headline: Misaki is attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720, analyzable as み (mi) plus 先 (saki, “tip, point; promontory”).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720.
Analyzable as a compound of み (mi, see below) + 先(さき) (saki, “tip, point; promontory”).
The mi prefix is likely the honorific prefix 御(み) (mi-), and the term misaki is attested explicitly with the spelling 御(み)碕(さき) (mi-saki) in the Nihon Shoki.
Alternative theories as to the identity of the み (mi) include:
* 水(み) (mi, “water”, bound prefix form of 水(みず) (mizu)), although the semantics this suggests may instead mean “water tip”, i.e. a jutting-out of water, not of land — an inlet.
* Shift from 海(うみ) (umi, “sea”), with the same consideration as above.

examples.en: The ship sailed around the cape.

examples.ja: 船は岬に沿って回った。
examples.en: The boat sailed around the promontory.

headline: Mune is from Proto-Japonic *munai, with the same apophony as 神 (kamu, kami).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *munai. The apophony is similar to the phonetic process observed in the shift from 神 (kamu, “spirit, god”, older form used in compounds) to 神 (kami, newer form, used as a standalone noun); see WT:AJPX#Standalone forms and combining forms.
Alternatively, may be a compound of 身 (mu, “body”) + 根 (ne, “root”). Other theories have been suggested.

The first edition of the Nihon Kokugo Daijiten says that this is cognate with 棟 (mune, “main roofline, roof ridge”) and 宗, 旨 (mune, “gist, main idea, primary part”), from the underlying idea of central or main portion. However, the accent of 胸 (mune) in the Heian period is HL, while the accent of 棟 (mune) is HH. This suggests that they may not be directly related.

Notably, 棟 and 宗 also have an older reading muna that is only used in compounds (for 宗, possibly only in place names). Meanwhile, 旨 (mune) (Heian HH) appears in The Tale of Genji of circa 1001-1004, and this reading is used as a standalone noun rather than in compounds. This is consistent with other nouns that have paired vowel forms, and suggests that muna is probably the original form, and that the compound derivation is a folk etymology.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

headline: Gyōretsu is attested from 749 as a line or procession; the date of its mathematical sense, “matrix”, is uncertain.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, in turn from Middle Chinese 行列 (MC haeng ljet). First attested in Japanese in 749.

The date of the mathematical sense is uncertain. Matrices for calculation were long known in Chinese mathematics, and were used to solve systems of linear equations in the work 九章算術 /九章算术 (“The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art”), compiled from the 10th through the 2nd centuries BCE. The component terms 行 and 列 (liè) are both used in that text, but not in the particular combination of 行列 (hángliè) (see also Wikisource). The first Japanese work on this aspect of mathematics was a 1683 text by 関孝和 (Seki Takakazu), but it is not yet clear if this text includes the term 行列 (gyōretsu) with the sense of matrix.

examples.ja: 行列が学校の側を通った。
彼は行列を見ようと首を伸ばした。
examples.en: He craned his neck to see the procession.

headline: Haka has no known origin; the final ka may be 処 (-ka, suffix denoting place), as in 住み処 (sumika).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *paka. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.
Ultimate derivation unknown. One possibility is that the final ka may be 処(か) (-ka, suffix denoting place), as in the term 住(す)み処(か) (sumika, “dwelling, home, abode”, literally “living place”).

examples.en: They buried him in his grave.

headline: Nendo is uncertain, possibly from Middle Chinese 年度.

sources.quote: Uncertain. Possibly from Middle Chinese 年度 (MC nen duH). Compare modern Mandarin 年度 (niándù).

examples.ja: 零細小売店などは新年度には利益を上げるでしょう。
examples.en: Mom-and-pop stores will turn a profit in the new fiscal year.

headline: Hō was once はふ (fafu) in kan'on and ほふ (fofu) in goon, reportedly used in general and Buddhist senses respectively.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 法 (MC pjop). Originally, the kan'on was はふ (fafu), and the goon was ほふ (fofu), although both became ほう (hō) in modern Japanese. It is suggested that the kan'on was used in the general senses, while the goon was used in Buddhist contexts.

examples.en: A new law has come into existence.

headline: Kimi is possibly a borrowing from the Sillan word for king, written 今 (kum), whose morpheme survives in Korean 임금 (imgeum).

sources.quote: ⟨ki₁mi₁⟩ → */kʲimʲi/ → /kimi/
From Old Japanese. Possibly a borrowing from the Sillan word for king, written with the character 今 (kum). The same morpheme survives in the second syllable of the Modern Korean word 임금 (imgeum).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 憧る (akugaru).

meaning: to hurry, to be in a hurry, to rush
headline: Isogu appears to be a root iso (“earnest? industrious?”) plus -gu, first attested as isogi in the Man'yōshū of 759.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Ultimately from Proto-Japonic *isonku. Appears to be root iso ("earnest? industrious?") + verb-forming suffix -gu of uncertain meaning. Cognate with archaic adjective 勤し (isoshi, “diligent, industrious, hard-working”) and modern verb 勤しむ (isoshimu, “to work diligently, industriously”), may also be related to adverb いそいそ (isoiso, “cheerfully, unreservedly”), verb 勇む (isamu, “to be in high spirits, to be encouraged”).
First attested as noun form isogi ("hurrying, rushing") in the Man'yōshū of 759.

headline: Genryō is a Middle Chinese compound: 原 (gen, “original”) plus 料 (ryō, “material”).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese compound 原料 (MC ngjwon lew): 原 (gen, “original”) + 料 (ryō, “material”)

examples.en: Japan is lacking in raw materials.

examples.ja: 日本は原料を輸入に頼っている。
examples.en: Japan depends on imports for raw materials.
